newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels hold out as world pressure grows.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels hold out as world pressure grows.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding 103 VIP captives at the Japanese embassy residence in Peru defied growing international pressure on Saturday as the hostage crisis moved into its 11th day.

President Alberto Fujimori's refusal to bow to rebel demands received full backing from the world's leading nations who promised to help the Peruvian government with "all the appropriate means that it could request."

In the strongest show yet of world condemnation of the hostage crisis, the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations and Russia issued a communique in Paris on Friday labeling the rebels as "terrorists".
In Lima, a special session of congress called by Fujimori voted overwhelmingly to give "full support to the government and (whatever) decisions it takes to solve this grave crisis."

The Peruvian leader called the session after extending special search and arrest powers for the army and police throughout the capital. Until Friday, the emergency powers -- which allow police to make arrests without search warrants -- had covered only the centre and industrial outskirts of Lima and part of Peru's mountain and jungle regions.
Despite growing pressure from outside, the roughly 20 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas holed up inside the Japanese ambassador's home showed no signs of crumbling.
For the first day since Monday the rebels released no hostages on Friday, in spite of reports that three hostages -- including Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja -- were seriously ill.

The roughly 20 heavily armed gunmen have booby-trapped the residence against possible attack and said they would not come out until the government pardoned about 400 jailed comrades. Armed rebels, including one woman guerrilla, appeared several times at windows on Friday.

Michel Minnig, head of the International Red Cross team which has tried to ease the hostages' ordeal, said on Friday the situation inside the residence was "very, very calm." The elegant residence remained without power, however, and rebels and hostages were again forced to use flashlights and candles after dark.
Outside the property in the fashionable district of San Isidro, police arrested three suspects they said had posed as street vendors to gather information for the MRTA.

Police said the three -- two women and a man -- were found with maps and false identity papers. One police source said: "We think they were looking for information to report back to the national committee" of the MRTA, whose guerrillas stormed a lavish party at the residence on Dec. 17.
Police have now arrested six people outside the residence for suspicion of being guerrillas.
As international pressure on the rebels hardened, rumours swirled in Lima that a military solution to the crisis was again being considered.

Peruvian intelligence sources told Reuters a U.S. spyplane had made high-altitude night flights over the residence and crack anti-terrorist units of the Peruvian police were training around a model of the building.

International support for Peru's "no concessions" stance on the crisis was a personal triumph for Fujimori who was earlier criticised by Japan for his approach to the siege. Japanese government officials said last week there were sharp differences between Tokyo and Fujimori who has spoken only once in public since the crisis began.
But it was Japan, whose nationals account for the largest number of hostages, after Peru, which led calls earlier on Friday for unity in resolving the crisis.

"It is clear that the international community should not condone terrorism," Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told a news conference in Tokyo. "It is also necessary ... to act as one to help resolve this crisis by setting free all the hostages peacefully, and at an early date."

The guerrillas have released about 400 captives since storming the building. They have kept those they consider most useful as bargaining chips including two Peruvian ministers, Japanese businessmen, a handful of foreign diplomats and the brother of Fujimori.
